title: Scaling Causal Reasoning with Increasingly Complex Causal Simulators
claim: Reasoning faces scale, representation and supervision challenges; incrementally built executable simulators that translate between code and language address each one.
layout: 2 panels, left challenges to right solution, C1–C3 badges linking them
description: The figure has two halves split by a vertical line. The left half shows a graph of many nodes and arrows for a complex causal system. Next to it is a green box titled 'Challenges in Causal Reasoning', with three labelled items: C1 scale of causal system, C2 nonexecutable representation, and C3 no true signal to learn from. Below is a counterfactual query about 'Drug Y' and 'tumor X' in purple, with a confused robot icon. The right half sits under a blue banner, 'Increasingly Complex Causal Simulators'. A dashed arrow marked C1 points right over three growing causal graphs. Beneath them, code snippets and knowledge boxes show formalizing knowledge into executable code (C2). On the far right, code is informalized into natural language, and an executable answer is compared with the robot's answer (C3). The same C1–C3 badges tie challenges to solutions. Lavender, blue and green boxes carry the colour.
caption: Overview of CauSim. (Left) Causal reasoning faces three challenges: [C1] scale, [C2] non-executable representations, and [C3] lack of ground-truth supervision. (Right) CauSim addresses these through increasingly complex causal simulators: SCMs are built incrementally to scale complexity [C1]; non-executable causal knowledge is formalized into executable code and executable SCMs are informalized into natural language [C2]; enabling causal supervision [C3]
abstract: Despite surpassing human performance across mathematics, coding, and other knowledge-intensive tasks, large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with causal reasoning. A core obstacle is the target data itself: causal systems are complex and often expressed in non-executable forms, while ground-truth answers to causal queries are inherently scarce. We introduce CauSim, a framework that turns causal reasoning from a scarce-label problem into a scalable supervised one. CauSim constructs increasingly complex causal simulators: executable structural causal models (SCMs), incrementally built by LLMs, that scale to globally complex systems while maintaining verifiable answers to causal queries. CauSim operates across representations by formalizing non-executable causal knowledge into code, enabling data augmentation, and translating executable SCMs into natural language, enabling supervision in previously difficult-to-supervise representations. We structure our research into two parts: (1) how to construct increasingly complex causal simulators, and (2) a systematic study of what CauSim enables, demonstrating generalization across representations, consistent gains from curriculum scaling and data volume, LLM self-improvement through self-generated simulators, and data augmentation via formalization of existing domain knowledge.
